rationale: Both threat models cover assets, boundaries, attackers, attack paths and phased mitigations well, and both correctly name prompt injection as the dominant threat and blast-radius limits as the main defense. The decisive difference is in the first-wave mitigations. A's v1 filesystem scope is application-level path validation inside the tool. That does nothing once the agent runs shell commands: an allowlisted 'cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa' or any subprocess escapes it. A defers OS sandboxing to v2, which undercuts its own claim that the blast radius is bounded. B ships an OS-level project jail (bubblewrap or seatbelt or a container) in v1 and correctly notes the jail's own bypasses as the reason for later VM isolation. B also adds controls A misses: pinning and hash-verifying the agent's policy config so a hijacked agent cannot rewrite its allowlist, an audit log the agent cannot modify, and TLS enforcement on the model channel. Later it adds dependency freshness vetting, git-worktree isolation with auto-revert, and a session timeout and kill switch. Its residual-risk section gives a concrete example of abuse within allowed commands. A's untrusted-content tagging and explicit git approvals are good, but B's design is more sound.
